identity.title: Glucocorticoid exposure / abrupt withdrawal, known adrenal disease, hyperpigmentation

technique.how: Ask specifically about any glucocorticoid in the past year: oral, inhaled, intra-articular/epidural injections, topical, nasal, and megestrol or opioids; dose, duration, and whether it was recently stopped or missed. Ask about known Addison disease, pituitary disease, adrenalectomy, checkpoint-inhibitor or anticoagulant use, and look for mucosal/palmar-crease hyperpigmentation or vitiligo.
technique.prerequisites: Medication reconciliation including outside prescriptions and injections; collateral history if the patient is confused.

interpretation.positive_finding: Recent glucocorticoid exposure (especially higher dose, longer course, or abrupt stop) in a patient with unexplained hypotension, hyponatremia, hypoglycemia, or refractory shock makes adrenal insufficiency probable enough to treat empirically. Hyperpigmentation points to primary (ACTH-driven) disease.
interpretation.negative_finding: No steroid exposure and no known adrenal/pituitary disease lowers but does not exclude adrenal insufficiency (autoimmune, hemorrhage, infiltration, sepsis).
interpretation.pitfalls: Patients forget inhaled, injected, and topical steroids; exposure of any route, dose or duration cannot exclude suppression with certainty. Hyperpigmentation is absent in secondary/tertiary adrenal insufficiency.
interpretation.changes_what: Positive history in shock: draw cortisol/ACTH then give stress-dose hydrocortisone without waiting; negative history still warrants testing if hypotension, hyponatremia or hypoglycemia is unexplained.

sources.citation: Broersen LH, Pereira AM, Jorgensen JO, Dekkers OM. Adrenal Insufficiency in Corticosteroids Use: Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis. J Clin Endocrinol Metab. 2015.

Bornstein SR, Allolio B, Arlt W, Barthel A, Don-Wauchope A, Hammer GD, Husebye ES, Merke DP, et al. Diagnosis and Treatment of Primary Adrenal Insufficiency: An Endocrine Society Clinical Practice Guideline. J Clin Endocrinol Metab. 2016.

safety_scope.do_not_use_when: Do not withhold empiric hydrocortisone in suspected adrenal crisis because the steroid history is negative or uncertain.
safety_scope.escalation_warning: Hypotension unresponsive to fluids/vasopressors with a steroid history: treat as adrenal crisis immediately (IV hydrocortisone, saline, glucose).
safety_scope.interobserver_note: History item; no reliability data found.

extraction_notes: No diagnostic-accuracy study (sens/spec/LR) of the steroid-exposure history for adrenal insufficiency in acutely ill patients was found; the only quantitative evidence is post-test probability of biochemical AI among steroid-exposed patients from the Broersen 2015 meta-analysis (PMID 25844620), which has no sens/spec/LR field to hold it, so estimates[] is empty and the numbers are recorded here (all Abstract, Results): dose 'from 2.4% (95% CI, 0.6-9.3) (low dose) to 21.5% (95% CI, 12.0-35.5) (high dose)'; duration 'from 1.4% (95% CI, 0.3-7.4) (<28 d) to 27.4% (95% CI, 17.7-39.8) (>1 year) in asthma patients'; by route 'from 4.2% for nasal administration (95% CI, 0.5-28.9) to 52.2% for intra-articular administration (95% CI, 40.5-63.6)'; by disease 'from 6.8% for asthma with inhalation corticosteroids only (95% CI, 3.8-12.0) to 60.0% for hematological malignancies (95% CI, 38.0-78.6)'. Endocrine Society guideline (PMID 26760044) supports a low diagnostic and therapeutic threshold in acutely ill patients with predisposing factors; hyperpigmentation frequency is not quantified in the sources reviewed. Crossref DOI for Broersen not returned by the tool; PMID confirmed.
